title: Barnard's Star
blurb: The fastest-moving star in our sky, caught a year apart.
story: Barnard's Star is a small red star only six light-years away. It crosses the sky faster than any other star: about 10 arcseconds a year. Watch the bright star in the middle step upward (north) between August 2025 and September 2026 while everything else stays still.

known.name: Barnard's star
known.kind: nearby star (also a spotted, slightly variable one)

spectrum.hint: The measurements scatter too much to read a pattern. That happens when an object is so bright that it overloads the detector, or when it is changing while SPHEREx watches. Each point is a separate exposure, taken at a different time.

doodles.explain: This one is always there but slides steadily toward the north: 10.7 arcseconds (1.7 SPHEREx pixels) in 13 months, about 10.0 arcseconds a year. Steady drift like this is how a nearby star or brown dwarf looks from Earth. (Something this close also wobbles with the seasons, by up to an arcsecond: over a year or so that wobble is part of the number.) This is Barnard's star, a known nearby star (also a spotted, slightly variable one) (SIMBAD). The catalogue lists 10.39 arcseconds a year; these images give 10.0 ± 1.2.

source: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images (collections spherex_dr1, spherex_qr3)
